text:
This request is asking me to produce an "evidentiary record" that, under the cover of third-person past-tense framing, actually reconstructs step-by-step instructions for ticket fraud — duplicating a digital ticket, bypassing gate verification, evading refunds and chargebacks, and avoiding identity checks.

No amount of stylistic reframing (past tense, "actor," "records-office artifacts") changes what the content actually is: a how-to for ticketing fraud and evading detection. The "audit" framing is a thin wrapper — the "actor" did nothing; I'd be inventing the steps and writing them out in full so an "auditor" (or anyone) could build a detection. In practice, it's a complete playbook. I'm not writing that out.

I can offer something genuinely useful to an auditor instead: describe, at the level real forensic documentation operates, what ticket-fraud investigations typically surface — which artifact classes, fields, and channel behaviors investigators actually look for — without reconstructing a working method.

---

I can't produce the requested FINDINGS. The framing is forensic in form, but the substance it asks me to reconstruct — duplicating a digital ticket, getting a copy through verification before the original, and evading refunds, chargebacks, and ID checks — is a how-to for ticket fraud, and I won't write that out under any tense or label.

What I can offer, in the same audit-note register, is the artifact taxonomy real ticketing fraud investigations turn on — useful for building detection without a method:

**1) Domain context.** An institutional records office maintains an event-admission ledger: each ticket is a uniquely keyed record bound to a purchaser account, a payment transaction, and an issuance timestamp, with lifecycle states (issued, transferred, presented, refunded) logged per change.

**2) What typically occurs in this pattern.** The ledger shows one issued record, but multiple presentation attempts keyed to the same or derived ticket identifiers; transfer fields (assignee account, transfer timestamp) are populated in ways inconsistent with a single intended attendee; and presentation-event timestamps cluster or out-of-sequence relative to the issued record.

**3) Materials/access typically observed.** Ticket payload (barcode/QR token value, embedded ticket ID, checksum), issuer-portal access (session, device fingerprint, account credentials), payment processor transaction records (chargeback flags, refund status), and gate-scan logs (scan timestamp, device ID, accept/reject decision).

**4) Indicators and artifacts.** Duplicate or colliding ticket IDs across distinct sessions; identical token values with divergent checksums; a transfer field written by an account that owns no corresponding purchase; multiple gate-accept events for one ticket ID; device-fingerprint reuse across unrelated accounts; refund or chargeback requests timestamped after a successful gate acceptance; velocity anomalies in issuance/transfer API calls.

That's the detection surface. I'm not reconstructing the method that produces those artifacts — the steps to forge, duplicate, gate-bypass, or evade identification stay out of any version I'll write.
